- Right: (d) A loop where the model picks actions, they are run, and results come back — this is exactly the structure: the model requests a tool call, the program runs it, the result goes back into the model's next turn, and this repeats until the model has enough to answer. That repeating cycle, not anything about size or memory, is what makes a system an agent.
- (a) is wrong because a longer, more detailed prompt only changes what one call can do (e.g. more precise rules for how to use check_calendar), not whether the system loops; you could give that same long prompt to a single-shot model that never gets a second turn, and it still would not be an agent.
- (b) is wrong because automatic memory of every earlier conversation is neither guaranteed nor what defines an agent — your makerspace assistant could run the full pick-action/run/return loop within one conversation and still forget everything the moment the session ends; memory and looping are separate features.
- (c) is wrong because a bigger context window just lets one call hold more text (say, a whole machine manual); it still answers in a single shot unless the program wraps it in the pick-action/run/return loop.

- Right: (c) A request naming check_calendar, with the laser cutter and tomorrow's date as arguments — when the model decides to use a tool, all it ever outputs is a structured call like this; it never touches the booking system directly.
- You chose (a) "The calendar entries, which it read by opening the booking system on its own" — this treats the model as if it can reach out and browse the calendar itself. It can't: the model only ever produces text, and here that text is a tool request, not calendar data. The program is the thing with real access to the booking system; it runs check_calendar on the model's behalf and only then hands the entries back to the model. This is the same belief behind your answer to q4 — that the model carries out the action itself — so it is one idea to fix, not two.
- (b) is wrong because it is the model, not the program, that decides a tool is needed; the program is not scanning the question for words like "booking" and calling check_calendar on its own — it only runs the call once the model has explicitly asked for it.
- (d) is wrong for the same reason as (a): the model never receives or runs check_calendar's Python code. It only ever sees the tool's name, description and parameters (this is exactly what q6 asks about), and outputs a request to call it; the program's code is what actually executes.

- Right: (b) A step limit that stops the loop and reports what happened so far — once the agent is repeating the same edit against the same failing test, more steps with the same context will not change the outcome; a stopping condition is what turns an open-ended loop into something a person can safely take over.
- (a) is wrong because the problem here is not that something fails to fit in context — all 40 steps already fit. A larger window would just let it keep repeating itself for even longer before anyone notices.
- (c) is wrong because nothing about running the same failing edit a 41st time makes it more likely to succeed; without a change in information or strategy the loop has no reason to converge, and assuming it eventually will is exactly the mistake a step limit exists to guard against.
- (d) is wrong because the issue is not motivation, it is that the model keeps making the same decision from the same inputs; telling it to "try much harder" does not change what is in its context or give it a reason to try something different.

- Wrong: the correct count is 4 model calls, and your answer of 1 is off.
- Why: each model call ends in exactly one thing — a single tool request or the final answer, per the question's setup. Here that is: call 1 → requests check_calendar, call 2 → requests search_manuals, call 3 → requests check_training_record, call 4 → writes the final answer. Three tool requests plus one final answer is four calls.
- Your reasoning ("it runs the 3 tools itself and answers") is the same misconception as your answer to q2: that the model carries out tool calls directly instead of asking the program to run them and reporting back. The three tools are actually run by the program, in between model calls, not by the model, and each time a result comes back the model has to be called again just to see that result and decide what happens next. That is why having 3 tools to run adds 3 extra calls instead of 0 — running a tool is never free inside the loop, because it always costs a round trip back to the model.

- Right: "it sends it back to the model" — that much is correct, the tool's result does get fed back into the model's next input.
- Missing: the why. Full credit needs both parts — what happens (the result goes to the model) and why (so the model can use it to decide what to do next: another tool call, or the final answer). Your answer stops after the "what" and does not say what happens once the model has the result.
- Why this matters: without calling the model again with the result, the result would just sit inside the program with nothing done about it. It's like a teammate handing you a document and then never checking back in with you about it — the information exists, but nothing happens with it until it gets back to whoever is deciding the next move. Naming that "next step" purpose is what q6's answer also depends on: the model can only pick its next action from what is actually in front of it.

- Right: you correctly said the model gets a list of tools, each with a name and a description of what it does, and picks the one that fits — that is exactly how tool selection works, from the descriptions the program gives it, never from reading any code.
- Wrong: the added claim that "it also remembers on its own which tool it picked for questions like that in earlier sessions" is not true, and it is an extra claim beyond what the question asked.
- Why: a model has no built-in memory of past sessions — each call only knows what is actually sitting in its current context, nothing more. If this were true, your makerspace assistant would "just know" that a returning student already asked about the laser cutter last week without anyone telling it — the same way a cashier who has never met you would somehow already know your usual order on your first visit. In fact, every session starts from nothing unless the program deliberately saves something (a note in a file, a database row) and feeds it back in later; that is a design choice the program makes, not something the model does on its own. This is the exact belief behind option (b) in q1, "automatic memory of every earlier conversation" — you correctly rejected it there when it was offered as a choice, but it resurfaced here, attached specifically to tool selection, when you had to generate the answer yourself.

summary: You have the agent loop itself down solid: q1 and q3 show you can name the pick-action/run/return cycle and recognize that a stopping condition, not a bigger model or a longer prompt, is what saves a stuck loop. The idea to fix first is M4, the belief that the model carries out tool calls itself (the laser-cutter calendar, the three tools in q4) rather than only ever requesting them — this cost you q2 and q4, both from the same root belief, and it is the exact gap learning record 0002 flagged as not yet checked. A second, quieter version of a similar belief, M3 (the model remembers automatically across sessions), surfaced in q6 even though you correctly ruled it out as an option in q1 — it seems to come back when you have to generate an answer rather than just recognize one. Next step: trace the laser-cutter example from q2 end to end on paper, writing down literally what text the model outputs at each step (a tool request, then later the final answer) and what text the program sends back — that should make it concrete that the model only ever produces and reads text, never code or calendar entries directly.
